ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Study 1 received approval from the University of Western Australia Ethics Committee on 10 February 2025 (Project Identifier: 2025/ET000124).
All methods were conducted in accordance with the National Statement on Ethical Conduct in Human Research (NHMRC/ARC/Universities Australia) and the Declaration of Helsinki.
A convenience sample of 200 human participants was recruited from Prolific between 27 and 31 March 2026 (94 men, 102 women, 3 non-binary and 1 questioning; aged 22-69, M = 41.6, SD = 13.2).
Participants were pre-screened to be located in the USA and to have English as a first language.
After providing informed consent to participate in the study, participants were shown an instructions page adapted from the prompt used to generate the LLM ratings of the same claims (see Table 4).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Types of Truth: How Subjective & Objective Truth Guide Belief Change
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
Baseline: Perceived truth (human ratings) will positively predict belief update (known from Fay et al., 2026: https://psycnet.apa.org/fulltext/2026-68146-001.html)
Hypothesis 1: Objective truth (aggregated LLM ratings) will positively predict belief update above and beyond perceived truth (human ratings).
Hypothesis 2: There will be an interaction such that the effect of perceived truth on belief update will vary as a function of objective truth.
table.design_dependent_variables:
The primary dependent variable (DV) is belief update. This DV is drawn from Experiment 3 of Fay et al. (2026) (https://psycnet.apa.org/fulltext/2026-68146-001.html).

Belief update is operationalised as participants' self-reported change in belief regarding the target claim after reading a message associated with that claim. Consistent with Fay et al. (2026), belief update was computed as the difference between participants' post-message belief rating and their initial belief rating following presentation of the claim alone. Ratings ranged from −50 to 50, with positive values indicating belief change in the direction advocated by the message, negative values indicating change away from the message position, and values near zero indicating little or no change in belief.
table.study_design_overview:
The study re-analyses existing data from Experiment 3 of Fay et al. (2026) (https://psycnet.apa.org/fulltext/2026-68146-001.html).

A key feature of the present study is the construction of a new IV that indexes "objective truth".  It is derived by having four large language models (LLMs) independently rate the truthfulness of each message on a 5-point Likert Scale (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity). Provided there is sufficient inter-rater agreement among the LLMs (Krippendorff's α > .60), their truth ratings will be averaged to create a continuous, message-level measure of objective truth.  This variable is not part of the original Fay et al. (2026) dataset and is newly generated for the present study.
table.statistical_tests:
Linear mixed-effects regression models will be used to predict belief update (DV).  All models will be estimated using maximum likelihood and will include crossed random intercepts for message producers and message claims.

Three nested models will be estimated:
1. Subjective truth model (baseline model)
m1_belief <- lmer(Belief.Update ~ Truth_Human_Rating_c + (1 | producer) + (1 | claim), data = TypesOfTruth, REML = FALSE)
2. Additive model (objective truth main effect)
m2_belief <- lmer(Belief.Update ~ Truth_Human_Rating_c + LLMs_Truth_Rating_c + (1 | producer) + (1 | claim), data = TypesOfTruth, REML = FALSE)
3. Interaction model
m3_belief <- lmer(Belief.Update ~ Truth_Human_Rating_c*LLMs_Truth_Rating_c + (1 | producer) + (1 | claim), data = TypesOfTruth, REML = FALSE)

Hypothesis testing.  Likelihood ratio tests will be used to compare model fit across these nested models in R using:
anova(m1_belief, m2_belief, m3_belief)
table.outliers_and_exclusions: No participants or messages will be excluded based on performance, response patterns, or statistical properties (e.g., accuracy, extremity, or influence). The dataset from Fay et al. (2026), Experiment 3 will be analysed in full.
table.sample_size: The sample size for human participants is fixed by the original study design and data availability.

table.formatted: Standardized loadings were uniformly high, ranging from .811 to .918 in Study 2 and from .842 to .881 in Study 3 (all ps < .001).

table.formatted: Adding LLM-derived objective truthfulness significantly improved model fit, χ²(1) = 42.58, p < .001, with the explained variance increasing from R² = .317 to R² = .330 (ΔR² = .013), indicating that objective truthfulness accounted for additional variance in belief change beyond perceived truthfulness.
table.expanded: Adding LLM-derived objective truthfulness significantly improved model fit, χ²(1) = 42.58, p < .001, with the explained variance increasing from R² = .317 to R² = .330 (ΔR² = .013), indicating that objective truthfulness accounted for additional variance in belief change beyond perceived truthfulness.

table.formatted: Including the interaction between perceived and objective truthfulness further improved model fit, χ²(1) = 47.99, p < .001, with the explained variance increasing to R² = .342 (ΔR² = .012), indicating that the association between perceived truthfulness and belief change varied as a function of objective truthfulness.
table.expanded: Including the interaction between perceived and objective truthfulness further improved model fit, χ²(1) = 47.99, p < .001, with the explained variance increasing to R² = .342 (ΔR² = .012), indicating that the association between perceived truthfulness and belief change varied as a function of objective truthfulness.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 159 columns across 14 data files.
#### Issues Identified

16 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 14 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 3 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  1 of 3 scripts ran without error when executed.
-  13 installable dependencies detected.
- 66 statistics stored from the extracted output; 0 of 37 reported tests matched (0%).

ethics_statements: Study 1 received approval from the University of Western Australia Ethics Committee on 10 February 2025 (Project Identifier: 2025/ET000124).
All methods were conducted in accordance with the National Statement on Ethical Conduct in Human Research (NHMRC/ARC/Universities Australia) and the Declaration of Helsinki.
live_data_statements: A convenience sample of 200 human participants was recruited from Prolific between 27 and 31 March 2026 (94 men, 102 women, 3 non-binary and 1 questioning; aged 22-69, M = 41.6, SD = 13.2).
Participants were pre-screened to be located in the USA and to have English as a first language.
After providing informed consent to participate in the study, participants were shown an instructions page adapted from the prompt used to generate the LLM ratings of the same claims (see Table 4).
Participants were allowed to progress to the main task after correctly answering a comprehension check question ("The claims should be rated as true or false based on...?"
In the main task, participants were shown the list of claims to be rated as true or false, randomly ordered and split over four pages.
Once participants had rated each claim and responded to the attention checks, the task was complete.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 3 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "—"), Basis = c("numeric", 
"numeric", "numeric")), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 3 scripts: 1 ran without error, 0 errored, 2 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

text.text: People must navigate socially transmitted information that varies from accurate to misleading or false.
Here, we examined how perceived and objective truth predict belief change across three studies.
In Study 1, four web-enabled frontier large language models (LLMs) and 200 human raters evaluated claims from two fact-checked datasets.
LLMs outperformed humans in inter-rater agreement and discriminative sensitivity, supporting their use as a scalable proxy for objective truth.
In Study 2 and 3, we applied this proxy to two large message corpora and examined its association with belief change.
Perceived truth and LLM-derived objective truth independently predicted belief change.

Moreover, objective truth moderated the association between perceived truth and belief change: the association between perceived truth and belief change was strongest for messages with lower objective truth and weakened as objective truth increased.
These findings suggest that belief change reflects both subjective truth evaluations and the correspondence of information with reality.
Truth is rarely one-dimensional, and different forms of truth may guide cognition and behaviour.
Take Sperber's classic observations of the Dorze, an Ethiopian Orthodox Christian community (Sperber, 1975).
text.formatted: Take Sperber's classic observations of the Dorze, an Ethiopian Orthodox Christian community <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Sperber, 1975)</ref>.

text.text: The Dorze believe that local leopards are also Orthodox Christians who observe religious fasts.
Yet, on fasting days, the Dorze still guard their livestock against leopard attacks.

Sperber resolves this apparent contradiction by considering the different functions beliefs serve: beliefs associated with religious or symbolic commitments need not guide behaviour in the same way as beliefs grounded in direct experience of the physical world.
In this way, symbolic beliefs are used to meet social and identity-related goals and factual beliefs are used to model reality and for behaving optimally within it (Van Leeuwen, 2014).
text.formatted: In this way, symbolic beliefs are used to meet social and identity-related goals and factual beliefs are used to model reality and for behaving optimally within it <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Van Leeuwen, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Empirical evidence indicates that people can distinguish between these types of truth: when accuracy is financially incentivised, Democratic and Republican political partisans give responses that more closely track factual information (Bullock et al., 2015; Rathje et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Empirical evidence indicates that people can distinguish between these types of truth: when accuracy is financially incentivised, Democratic and Republican political partisans give responses that more closely track factual information <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bullock et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Rathje et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Ultimately, human cognition must accommodate socially meaningful beliefs and beliefs oriented toward accurately representing the world.
The present study asks how different types of truth might guide belief change.
Most of what we know, we do not directly observe.

We rely on the testimony of others that black holes distort spacetime, that historical events such as the Battle of Bannockburn occurred, or that climate models accurately describe aspects of the Earth's climate-all without personally verifying these claims.

We must navigate the relationship between empiricism (Hume, 1748; Markie & Folescu, 2021)-where knowledge about the external world is grounded in experience and observation-and social constructionism (Berger & Luckmann, 1966; Burr & Dick, 2025), which emphasises how our knowledge and understanding of the world are collectively constructed and transmitted through social interaction.
text.formatted: We must navigate the relationship between empiricism <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Hume, 1748;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Markie & Folescu, 2021)</ref>-where knowledge about the external world is grounded in experience and observation-and social constructionism <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Berger & Luckmann, 1966;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Burr & Dick, 2025)</ref>, which emphasises how our knowledge and understanding of the world are collectively constructed and transmitted through social interaction.

text.text: This challenge is particularly acute in an era of pervasive misinformation and disinformation, in which socially transmitted information can be deliberately crafted to distort perceptions of reality (Ecker et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This challenge is particularly acute in an era of pervasive misinformation and disinformation, in which socially transmitted information can be deliberately crafted to distort perceptions of reality <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Ecker et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Because we routinely act on claims that we cannot personally verify, this creates an epistemic challenge: determining when socially transmitted information accurately tracks empirical reality.
Navigating this challenge is essential, particularly when high-stakes decisions depend on secondhand information rather than firsthand experience.
Epistemic vigilance is a framework for understanding how people navigate this challenge (Mercier, 2020; Sperber et al., 2010; see also Truth-Default Theory; Levine, 2014 Levine, , 2022)).
text.formatted: Epistemic vigilance is a framework for understanding how people navigate this challenge <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Mercier, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Sperber et al., 2010</ref>; see also Truth-Default Theory; <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Levine, 2014</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Levine, , 2022))</ref>.

text.text: Epistemic vigilance refers to a suite of cognitive mechanisms that enable people to evaluate the credibility of socially transmitted information and guard against being misled by others.

These mechanisms operate on the information source, such as whether a communicator is knowledgeable, trustworthy, or motivated to deceive, and on the message, including whether it is plausible and consistent with existing knowledge and experience.

Epistemic vigilance provides a bridge between socially acquired information and empirically grounded knowledge: although people necessarily depend on others for much of what they know, they do not simply accept what they are told.
Instead, they evaluate the epistemic quality of the communicated information and selectively incorporate it into their beliefs (e.g., Tamariz et al., 2014; Walker et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Instead, they evaluate the epistemic quality of the communicated information and selectively incorporate it into their beliefs (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Tamariz et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Walker et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: If these mechanisms function effectively, subjective assessments of message truth will provide a meaningful signal of objective truth: messages that are objectively more truthful should, on average, be perceived as more truthful.
From this perspective, truth evaluation functions as an epistemic filter through which socially transmitted information must pass before changing beliefs.

Recent research provides evidence that perceived truthfulness is an important predictor of social influence. Fay et al. (2026) examined the impact of persuasive messages designed to support a range of claims (e.g., 'Prisoners should be forced to undertake manual labour').

(2026)</ref> examined the impact of persuasive messages designed to support a range of claims (e.g., 'Prisoners should be forced to undertake manual labour').

text.text: Human participants and large language models (LLMs) were instructed to produce messages that were truthful, false, or unconstrained with respect to truth, generating a large corpus of messages (N > 4,500) that varied in their intended veracity.
text.formatted: Human participants and large language models (LLMs) were instructed to produce messages that were truthful, false, or unconstrained with respect to truth, generating a large corpus of messages (N > 4,500) that varied in their intended veracity.

text.text: Separate groups of human participants subsequently evaluated these messages on several psychological dimensions, including perceived truthfulness, positive emotion, persuasiveness, and belief change.
Messages intended to be truthful were, on average, perceived as more truthful, more persuasive, and more effective at changing beliefs than messages intended to be false.
Importantly, across the dimensions tested, perceived truthfulness was the strongest predictor of persuasion and belief change.
This finding is consistent with the possibility that perceived truthfulness functions as an effective epistemic filter.
However, it leaves two important questions unresolved: to what extent does perceived truthfulness correspond to objective truth, and to what extent do each predict belief change?
The present research addresses these questions by distinguishing between perceived and objective truthfulness.
We use the corpus of human-generated messages from Fay et al. (2026;  Experiment 1 and Experiment 3), together with the associated human ratings of perceived truthfulness and belief change.
text.formatted: We use the corpus of human-generated messages from <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Fay et al. (2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> Experiment 1 and Experiment 3), together with the associated human ratings of perceived truthfulness and belief change.

text.text: We then obtain an independent model-based estimate of each message's objective truthfulness by aggregating truth ratings from four frontier LLMs, each with web search capability, which we use as a proxy measure of objective truth.

Study 1 evaluates whether LLM truth ratings provide a reliable and criterion-valid proxy for objective truthfulness, examining their inter-model reliability and criterion validity against fact-checked datasets.

Study 2 tests the correspondence between perceived and objective truthfulness, and whether objective truthfulness predicts belief change above and beyond perceived truthfulness using the messages and ratings from Fay et al. (2026).
text.formatted: Study 2 tests the correspondence between perceived and objective truthfulness, and whether objective truthfulness predicts belief change above and beyond perceived truthfulness using the messages and ratings from <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Fay et al. (2026)</ref>.

text.text: Study 3 provides a preregistered direct replication of the Study 2 findings using an independent dataset from Fay et al. (2026) (https://aspredicted.org/mf4qb9.pdf).
text.formatted: Study 3 provides a preregistered direct replication of the Study 2 findings using an independent dataset from <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Fay et al. (2026)</ref> (<ref type="url" target="https://aspredicted.org/mf4qb9.pdf">https://aspredicted.org/mf4qb9.pdf</ref>).

text.text: Together, these studies distinguish between perceived and objective message truthfulness, allowing us to test whether perceived truthfulness provides an effective epistemic signal of objective reality and whether objective truthfulness contributes to belief change beyond the influence of perceived truth.

LLMs show promise as automated fact-checkers, particularly when they are able to retrieve and evaluate relevant external evidence, and demonstrate strong performance against established factual benchmarks (e.g., Quelle & Bovet, 2024; Renault et al., 2026; Rothermel et al., 2024).

text.text: People also show a capacity to discriminate between true and false information, with meta-analytic evidence showing that they judge fact-checked true news as substantially more accurate than fact-checked false news (Pfänder & Altay, 2025; Cohen's d = 1.12).

text.text: Study 1 asks whether LLMs can provide a reliable and valid proxy for objective truth.

We address this by comparing the truth judgements from four frontier LLMs (Claude, Gemini, GPT-5, and Perplexity), each with web-search capability, with those of 200 human participants who judged the same set of statements.

The LLMs and human truth judgements (true or false) were evaluated against gold-standard classifications from two fact-checked datasets, FEVER (Thorne et al., 2018) and TruthSeeker (Dadkhah et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The LLMs and human truth judgements (true or false) were evaluated against gold-standard classifications from two fact-checked datasets, FEVER <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Thorne et al., 2018)</ref> and TruthSeeker <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Dadkhah et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Study 1 received approval from the University of Western Australia Ethics Committee on 10 February 2025 (Project Identifier: 2025/ET000124).
Human participants viewed an information sheet before giving informed consent to take part in the study.
All methods were conducted in accordance with the National Statement on Ethical Conduct in Human Research (NHMRC/ARC/Universities Australia) and the Declaration of Helsinki.

Four frontier LLMs-Claude, Gemini, GPT-5 and Perplexity (see Table 1) -each configured to incorporate web searches to retrieve up-to-date information from trusted sources, assessed the truth of 106 fact-checked statements from the FEVER dataset (49 true, 57 false; Thorne et al., 2018) and 100 fact-checked statements from the TruthSeeker dataset (50 true, 50 false; Dadkhah et al., 2024).

text.text: A convenience sample of 200 human participants was recruited from Prolific between 27 and 31 March 2026 (94 men, 102 women, 3 non-binary and 1 questioning; aged 22-69, M = 41.6, SD = 13.2).
Participants were pre-screened to be located in the USA and to have English as a first language.
Each participant was randomly allocated to rate the truth of either the FEVER statements or the TruthSeeker statements (n = 100 each), and was paid £3 on completion of the study.

text.text: Your task is to evaluate the claim for factual accuracy.
Focus on identifying false, misleading, or unsubstantiated claims.
## Evaluation Process 1.
Determine if the claim is: -TRUE: Claim is supported by multiple credible sources with no significant contradicting evidence.
-FALSE: Claim is contradicted by clear evidence from credible sources.
-UNVERIFIABLE: Claim cannot be conclusively verified or refuted with available evidence.
## Guidelines -Remain politically neutral and focus solely on factual accuracy.
-Do not use political leaning as a factor in your evaluation.
-Prioritize official data, peer-reviewed research, and reports from credible institutions.
-Cite specific, reliable sources for your determinations.
-Consider the context and intended meaning of statements.
-Distinguish between factual claims and opinions.
-Pay attention to dates, numbers, and specific details.
-Be precise and thorough in your explanations.

Respond in JSON format (including json code block delimiters) with the following structure where "binary_rating" represents a two-alternative forced-choice response that best reflects your original rating: ```json { "rating": "TRUE|FALSE|UNVERIFIABLE", "binary_rating": "TRUE|FALSE" } ``` Ensure your evaluation is thorough, fair, and focused solely on factual accuracy.
Do not allow personal bias to influence your assessment.
Be especially rigorous with claims that sound implausible or extraordinary.

text.text: After providing informed consent to participate in the study, participants were shown an instructions page adapted from the prompt used to generate the LLM ratings of the same claims (see Table 4).

text.text: Participants were allowed to progress to the main task after correctly answering a comprehension check question ("The claims should be rated as true or false based on...?"
with possible responses "Their alignment with my political leaning," "Their factual accuracy" [the correct answer] and "Their word count").

To encourage the participants to make "natural" truth judgements, the instructions were deliberately non-specific about whether participants should respond based on their existing knowledge or look up the answers using external resources (e.g., using LLMs or via web search).

Participants spent an average of 3.2-39.3 seconds evaluating the truth of each claim (M = 8.8, SD = 4.9), so we consider it unlikely that participants looked up the answers to more than a small minority of questions, if any.
In the main task, participants were shown the list of claims to be rated as true or false, randomly ordered and split over four pages.
Each claim was displayed to the left of radio buttons marked "True" and "False".
Two attention checks were also included, one asking the participant to select "False" for that item to show that they were paying attention, and the other asking them to select "True".
The attention checks (presented in a random order) were placed one third and two thirds of the way through the list of claims.
Once participants had rated each claim and responded to the attention checks, the task was complete.
No participant failed the comprehension check or either of the two attention checks.
Completion time was approximately 13 minutes.

Inter-rater reliability and criterion validity were assessed to evaluate the consistency and discriminative accuracy of the LLM and human truth judgements across the two fact-checked datasets.

Inter-rater reliability indexed agreement in binary truth classifications (true, false) across raters, whereas criterion validity indexed correspondence with the fact-checked dataset classifications, which served as the criterion for truth classification.
LLMs demonstrated high inter-model agreement across both datasets, indicating strong convergence in their truth classifications (FEVER: α = 0.84; TruthSeeker: α = 0.73).
Human raters showed substantially lower agreement, with particularly weak agreement in the TruthSeeker dataset (FEVER: α = 0.31; TruthSeeker: α = 0.19).
So, LLMs showed substantially greater consistency in their truth classifications than human raters across both datasets.
Criterion validity was assessed using signal detection analysis, with sensitivity (dʹ) and response bias (C) estimated separately for the LLM and human raters (see Table 5 and Figure 1).
text.formatted: Criterion validity was assessed using signal detection analysis, with sensitivity (dʹ) and response bias (C) estimated separately for the LLM and human raters (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">5</ref> and Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: LLMs demonstrated substantially greater sensitivity than human raters across both datasets.
All four LLMs showed strong discriminative performance, with dʹ values exceeding 2.3 across datasets and exceeding 3.0 in the strongest cases.
By contrast, human performance was modest, with dʹ = 1.09 for FEVER and dʹ = 0.76 for TruthSeeker, indicating above-chance but limited discrimination between true and false claims.
Response bias (C) varied across models and datasets, with LLMs showing a more conservative criterion, particularly for TruthSeeker, whereas human raters showed relatively little bias.
Overall, LLMs showed high inter-model reliability and strong criterion validity, consistently outperforming human raters in discriminating between fact-checked true and false claims.
These findings support the validity of LLM-based truth ratings as a proxy for objective truth, which we use in Study 2 and 3 to predict belief change.
People can discriminate between binary true or false fact-checked news (Pfänder & Altay, 2025).
text.formatted: People can discriminate between binary true or false fact-checked news <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Pfänder & Altay, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, truthfulness is rarely binary and cannot always be established through fact-checking.

The information people share with others-from personal views on current affairs and social issues to claims about politics, sports, and popular culture-can vary continuously in its degree of truthfulness, ranging from outright falsehoods and misleading statements to partially accurate or entirely truthful content.

This distinction may be consequential for belief change: recent evidence suggests that outright false information on Facebook had little impact on COVID-19 vaccination rates, whereas truebut-misleading "gray-area" content reduced vaccination rates (Allen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This distinction may be consequential for belief change: recent evidence suggests that outright false information on Facebook had little impact on COVID-19 vaccination rates, whereas truebut-misleading "gray-area" content reduced vaccination rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Allen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: So, understanding belief change requires distinguishing not only between true and false information, but also between degrees of truthfulness. Fay et al. (2026) generated a large corpus of messages that vary in perceived truthfulness and other psychological dimensions, and showed that greater perceived message truthfulness was associated with stronger belief change.

(2026)</ref> generated a large corpus of messages that vary in perceived truthfulness and other psychological dimensions, and showed that greater perceived message truthfulness was associated with stronger belief change.

text.text: Because perceived and objective truthfulness are not necessarily equivalent, this leaves open the question of whether the belief change associated with more truthful messages reflects their perceived truthfulness, objective truthfulness or both types of truth.

text.text: In Experiment 1 and 3 of this study, human participants generated persuasive (Experiment 1) and attention-grabbing (Experiment 3) written messages (each no more than 280 characters) that supported 15 different claims (e.g., 'Singleuse plastic products should be banned'; N=285 human message producers in each experiment).

Message generation occurred under one of three conditions: instructed to produce true messages (i.e., statements they believed to be true), instructed to produce false messages (i.e., statements they believed to be false), or left unconstrained with respect to veracity.

A separate sample of human participants rated 9 of the 15 messages 1 generated by each human producer across multiple dimensions, including perceived truthfulness, persuasiveness, and belief change (N=1,710 message raters in Experiment 1 and N=1,710 message raters in Experiment 3).
Belief change was measured by the difference in participants' agreement with a claim before and after reading one of the messages.
This directly captures belief change, unlike the single measure of message persuasion, so we focus on belief change in the present study.
Message truthfulness was measured on a 5-point Likert scale ("To the best of your knowledge, how truthful is the post?", ranging from1 = not at all to5 = extremely).

Agreement with each claim (for the belief change measure) was rated before and after reading the associated message, using a 101-point scale ranging from -50 (strongly disagree) to +50 (strongly agree), with 0 representing a neutral position.
Belief change was calculated by subtracting pre-message agreement from post-message agreement, so that higher values indicate greater belief change in response to the message.
Each message received 10 independent ratings per dimension.
This procedure yielded a large corpus of unique messages (N=2,565 in Experiment 1 and N=2,565 in Experiment 3) that varied in perceived truthfulness and belief change (see Figure 2).
text.formatted: This procedure yielded a large corpus of unique messages (N=2,565 in Experiment 1 and N=2,565 in Experiment 3) that varied in perceived truthfulness and belief change (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: 1 To reduce the cost of having human raters evaluate a large corpus of messages, 9 out of 15 messages were sampled from each producer, and each message was rated by 10 independent raters.
In Study 2 and 3, we obtained truthfulness ratings for the full corpus of messages using four frontier LLMs, each with a web-search capability enabled.
The claim stimuli used in Study 1, drawn from the FEVER and TruthSeeker datasets, were uniformly single-sentence statements, each of which was factcheckable in principle.

In contrast, the corpus of messages produced in Fay et al. (2026), which were designed to persuade (Study 2), or to capture attention (Study 3), varied considerably, both in the number of claims being made within a message, and the degree to which these claims could reasonably be fact-checked.

text.text: For a given message, each LLM was instructed to extract any single-clause claim being made, to fact-check each claim and rate its truthfulness using a four-point Likert scale ("TRUE", "FALSE", "MISLEADING", "UNVERIFIABLE" ), and finally to provide an overall rating of message truthfulness using a five-point Likert scale ("NOT_AT_ALL", "SLIGHTLY", "SOMEWHAT", "VERY_MUCH", and "EXTREMELY" ).
Following the same procedure as Study 1, LLM responses were collected using a Python script that exercised the respective API for each model.
However, while we used the same model families as in Study 1, the exact model version differed -see Table 6 for model version and processing dates.

-UNVERIFIABLE: Claim cannot be conclusively verified or refuted with available evidence.
How truthful is the post overall? -NOT_AT_ALL: All claims are obviously false or misleading.
-SLIGHTLY: Most claims are false or misleading, significantly distorting the facts, but some parts of the post may be true.
-SOMEWHAT: The post contains a roughly equal mix of true and false/misleading claims.
-VERY_MUCH: Most claims are true, with minor inaccuracies that don't affect the main message.
-EXTREMELY: All claims are verifiable and true.
## Guidelines -Remain politically neutral and focus solely on factual accuracy.
-Do not use political leaning as a factor in your evaluation.
-Prioritize official data, peer-reviewed research, and reports from credible institutions.
-Cite specific, reliable sources for your determinations.
-Consider the context and intended meaning of statements.
-Distinguish between factual claims and opinions.
-Pay attention to dates, numbers, and specific details.
-Be precise and thorough in your explanations.

Respond in the following json format (including json code block delimiters): ```json { "summary": "Brief summary of your overall findings", "claims": [ // One entry for each fact-checked claim in the given post { "claim": "The first fact-checked claim", "rating": "TRUE|FALSE|MISLEADING|UNVERIFIABLE", "explanation": "Your explanation with supporting evidence", "sources": ["Source 1", "Source 2"] }, ...
// Additional claims ], "overall_truth_rating": "NOT_AT_ALL|SLIGHTLY|SOMEWHAT|VERY_MUCH|EXTREMELY" } ``` Ensure your evaluation is thorough, fair, and focused solely on factual accuracy.
Do not allow personal bias to influence your assessment.
Be especially rigorous with claims that sound implausible or extraordinary.
The Study 2 and 3 data were analysed using linear mixed-effects models.
Continuous fixed effects (perceived and objective truth) were grand-mean centred prior to analysis.
The random-effects structure included by-producer and by-claim random intercepts.

Model comparisons were conducted to evaluate incremental explanatory value, contrasting a perceived truth-only model, an additive model including perceived and objective truth, and a full interaction model (perceived × objective truth) in predicting belief change.
LLM-derived truthfulness ratings showed considerably greater agreement than human ratings.
In Study 2, agreement among the LLMs was moderate (Krippendorff's α = .63) and agreement among the human raters was low (α = .16).
Study 3 replicated this pattern, with much higher agreement among the LLMs (α = 0.66) compared to the human raters (α = 0.19).
The consistent convergence across LLMs in Study 2 and 3 supports the use of LLM truth ratings as a reliable message-level proxy for objective truthfulness.
Figure 3 shows the correlations between the LLM-derived objective truthfulness ratings and the human-rated perceived truthfulness ratings and belief change scores in Studies 2 and 3.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref> shows the correlations between the LLM-derived objective truthfulness ratings and the human-rated perceived truthfulness ratings and belief change scores in Studies 2 and 3.

text.text: The moderate correlations between the LLM-derived truthfulness ratings and the human-rated truthfulness ratings (r ≈ .47-.51 in Study 2; r ≈ .45-.51 in Study 3) indicate substantial correspondence between modelbased and human judgements of truth, consistent with the operation of epistemic vigilance whereby perceived message truthfulness provides a signal of objective truthfulness.

Belief change was more strongly correlated with human-rated perceived truthfulness (r = .48 in Study 2; r = .55 in Study 3) than with any individual LLM-derived truthfulness rating (r ≈ .24-.34 in Study 2; r ≈ .26-.36 in Study 3).
The LLM truthfulness ratings were strongly intercorrelated (r ≈ .61-.73 in Study 2; r ≈ .61-.71 in Study 3), indicating substantial convergence across models.
To further examine whether the LLM ratings captured a common underlying construct of objective truthfulness, we conducted confirmatory factor analyses separately in Studies 2 and 3.

In both studies, a one-factor model showed excellent fit (Study 2: χ²(2) = 6.72, CFI = 1.00, TLI = 1.00, RMSEA = .032, SRMR = .008; Study 3: χ²(2) = 1.86, CFI = 1.00, TLI = .999, RMSEA = .027, SRMR = .004).
Standardized loadings were uniformly high, ranging from .811 to .918 in Study 2 and from .842 to .881 in Study 3 (all ps < .001).
text.formatted: Standardized loadings were uniformly high, ranging from .811 to .918 in Study 2 and from .842 to .881 in Study 3 (all ps < .001).

text.text: So, the four LLM ratings appear to capture a common underlying dimension of objective truthfulness, providing support for their aggregation into a single message-level estimate.
We constructed an LLM-based objective truth proxy by averaging the LLM truthfulness ratings for each message.
In Study 2, a multilevel model showed that perceived (human-rated) truthfulness significantly predicted belief change.

Adding LLM-derived objective truthfulness significantly improved model fit, χ²(1) = 42.58, p < .001, with the explained variance increasing from R² = .317 to R² = .330 (ΔR² = .013), indicating that objective truthfulness accounted for additional variance in belief change beyond perceived truthfulness.
text.formatted: Adding LLM-derived objective truthfulness significantly improved model fit, χ²(1) = 42.58, p < .001, with the explained variance increasing from R² = .317 to R² = .330 (ΔR² = .013), indicating that objective truthfulness accounted for additional variance in belief change beyond perceived truthfulness.

text.text: Including the interaction between perceived and objective truthfulness further improved model fit, χ²(1) = 47.99, p < .001, with the explained variance increasing to R² = .342 (ΔR² = .012), indicating that the association between perceived truthfulness and belief change varied as a function of objective truthfulness.
text.formatted: Including the interaction between perceived and objective truthfulness further improved model fit, χ²(1) = 47.99, p < .001, with the explained variance increasing to R² = .342 (ΔR² = .012), indicating that the association between perceived truthfulness and belief change varied as a function of objective truthfulness.

text.text: Simple-slope analyses showed that perceived truthfulness significantly and positively predicted belief change across the observed range of objective truthfulness (see Figure 4 Panel A).
text.formatted: Simple-slope analyses showed that perceived truthfulness significantly and positively predicted belief change across the observed range of objective truthfulness (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref> Panel A).

text.text: The association was strongest when objective truthfulness was low (-1 SD; b = 7.33, SE = 0.29, t = 25.10, p < .001), remained substantial at the mean level of objective truthfulness (b = 6.07, SE = 0.25, t = 24.46, p < .001), and was weaker but still significant when objective truthfulness was high (+1 SD; b = 4.80, SE = 0.32, t = 14.95, p < .001).
text.formatted: The association was strongest when objective truthfulness was low (-1 SD; b = 7.33, SE = 0.29, t = 25.10, p < .001), remained substantial at the mean level of objective truthfulness (b = 6.07, SE = 0.25, t = 24.46, p < .001), and was weaker but still significant when objective truthfulness was high (+1 SD; b = 4.80, SE = 0.32, t = 14.95, p < .001).

text.text: Study 3 replicated this pattern of results using an independent dataset.

Perceived truthfulness significantly predicted belief change, and adding LLM-derived objective truthfulness significantly improved model fit, χ²(1) = 27.05, p < .001, with the explained variance increasing from R² = .381 to .388 (ΔR² = .007).
text.formatted: Perceived truthfulness significantly predicted belief change, and adding LLM-derived objective truthfulness significantly improved model fit, χ²(1) = 27.05, p < .001, with the explained variance increasing from R² = .381 to .388 (ΔR² = .007).

text.text: So, objective truthfulness again accounted for additional variance in belief change beyond perceived truthfulness.
Including the interaction between perceived and objective truthfulness further improved model fit, χ²(1) = 39.33, p < .001, increasing the explained variance to R² = .397 (ΔR² = .009).
text.formatted: Including the interaction between perceived and objective truthfulness further improved model fit, χ²(1) = 39.33, p < .001, increasing the explained variance to R² = .397 (ΔR² = .009).

text.text: As per Study 2, simple-slope analyses showed that perceived truthfulness significantly and positively predicted belief change across the observed range of objective truthfulness (see Figure 4, Panel B).
text.formatted: As per Study 2, simple-slope analyses showed that perceived truthfulness significantly and positively predicted belief change across the observed range of objective truthfulness (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>, Panel B).

text.text: The association was strongest when objective truthfulness was low (-1 SD; b = 9.73, SE = .33, t = 29.25, p < .001), remained substantial at the mean level of objective truthfulness (b = 8.41, SE = .27, t = 30.79, p < .001), and was weaker but still significant when objective truthfulness was high (+1 SD; b = 7.10, SE = .35, t = 20.03, p < .001).
text.formatted: The association was strongest when objective truthfulness was low (-1 SD; b = 9.73, SE = .33, t = 29.25, p < .001), remained substantial at the mean level of objective truthfulness (b = 8.41, SE = .27, t = 30.79, p < .001), and was weaker but still significant when objective truthfulness was high (+1 SD; b = 7.10, SE = .35, t = 20.03, p < .001).

text.text: Three robustness analyses indicated that these findings were robust to the aggregation of both the LLM-derived objective truthfulness ratings and the human perceived-truthfulness ratings, as well as to controlling for participants' initial agreement with the claim.
First, analyses using each individual LLM's truthfulness ratings separately produced the same pattern of results as those using the averaged LLM objective-truthfulness proxy.

Second, given the relatively low inter-rater reliability among the human perceived-truth ratings, we repeated the analyses using the unaggregated humanlevel observations, retaining each participant's individual perceived-truthfulness and belief-change ratings rather than averaging across raters for each message.
These analyses likewise produced the same pattern of results.
Third, using the unaggregated human-level observations, we repeated the analyses predicting subsequent agreement while controlling for participants' initial agreement with the claim.

These analyses also produced the same pattern of results, indicating that the effects of perceived and objective truthfulness were not attributable to differences in participants' initial agreement (see Supplement 2 for the results of each robustness test).

Overall, belief change was associated with human perceived truthfulness and LLM-derived objective truthfulness, with the strongest association observed for perceived truthfulness and a smaller but reliable contribution from objective truthfulness.

The interaction between the two indicated that the association between perceived truthfulness and belief change was strongest when objective truthfulness was low and weakened as objective truthfulness increased.
The present research examined how perceived and objective message truthfulness contributes to belief change.

Across three studies, we found that search-enabled frontier LLMs provide a reliable and valid proxy for objective truth; that aggregate human perceptions of message truthfulness correspond with LLM-derived objective truthfulness; and that perceived and objective truthfulness each independently predict belief change.

Importantly, objective truthfulness moderated the association between perceived truthfulness and belief change: perceived truthfulness was most strongly associated with belief change when objective truthfulness was relatively low, and this association weakened as objective truthfulness increased.
These findings replicated across independent datasets and individual LLMs.
Together, they suggest that belief change reflects both the correspondence of a message with objective reality and the recipient's subjective evaluation of its truthfulness.
Study 1 established the basis for using LLM-derived truth ratings as a proxy for objective truth.

Across two fact-checked datasets (FEVER and TruthSeeker), four frontier LLMs showed high intermodel convergence (α = .84 and .73), substantially exceeding agreement among human raters (α = .31 and .19).
They also demonstrated approximately three times greater discriminative sensitivity than human raters.

This pattern extended to the continuous, non-fact-checked message corpora used in Studies 2 and 3, where inter-LLM agreement was moderate (α = .63 and .66) but again far exceeded human agreement (α = .16 and .19).
Together, these results support the use of LLM ratings as a scalable, message-level operational proxy for objective truthfulness.
In Studies 2 and 3, aggregate human truthfulness ratings showed a moderate correspondence with LLM-derived objective truthfulness evaluations (r ≈ .45-.51).

This is consistent with the central premise of epistemic vigilance (Mercier, 2020; Sperber et al., 2010): people do not simply absorb socially transmitted information, but evaluate its plausibility and use these judgements to guide their beliefs.
text.formatted: This is consistent with the central premise of epistemic vigilance <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Mercier, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Sperber et al., 2010)</ref>: people do not simply absorb socially transmitted information, but evaluate its plausibility and use these judgements to guide their beliefs.

text.text: This is important because it places empiricism and social constructionism in a complementary relationship, bridging a long-standing rift between the disciplines (Gergen, 1973; Jost & Kruglanski, 2002).
text.formatted: This is important because it places empiricism and social constructionism in a complementary relationship, bridging a long-standing rift between the disciplines <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Gergen, 1973;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Jost & Kruglanski, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Much knowledge about the external world is necessarily socially acquired, consistent with the social construction of knowledge, but the usefulness of that knowledge ultimately depends in part on whether socially transmitted information tracks empirical reality.
Our findings suggest that aggregate human perceptions of message truthfulness generally track, but are imperfectly aligned with, objective truthfulness.
This imperfect alignment is consequential because it allows perceived and objective message truthfulness to provide partially distinct sources of information for belief change.
The central finding of Study 2 and 3 is that while perceived and objective truthfulness are moderately correlated, each makes a distinct contribution to belief change.

Perceived truth was the stronger predictor in both studies, but adding objective truthfulness led to a modest but statistically significant improvement to model fit beyond perceived truthfulness alone, indicating that objectively truer messages were associated with greater belief change even after accounting for perceived truthfulness.

Adding the perceived truthfulness by objective truthfulness interaction further improved model fit in both studies, indicating that the association between perceived truthfulness and belief change varied as a function of objective truthfulness.

Perceived truthfulness showed the strongest association with belief change when objective truthfulness was relatively low, with this association progressively weakening as objective truthfulness increased.
This suggests that perceived truthfulness provides a particularly important epistemic cue when information has a weaker correspondence with objective reality.
In such cases, people may rely more heavily on their existing knowledge, expectations, and evaluations of credibility when deciding whether information should be incorporated into their beliefs.
Conversely, when information more closely corresponds with objective reality, this diminishes the contribution of subjective perceptions of message truthfulness to belief change.
These findings suggest that belief change reflects both the properties of communicated information and the recipient's epistemic evaluation of those properties.
Our findings challenge the binary true-versus-false distinction that has dominated much misinformation research.
Such a distinction was uncommon in our message corpora, with few messages rated as outright true ('Extremely Truthful') or false ('Not at All Truthful'; see Figure 2 Truth ratings).
text.formatted: Such a distinction was uncommon in our message corpora, with few messages rated as outright true ('Extremely Truthful') or false ('Not at All Truthful'; see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref> Truth ratings).

text.text: Real-world information often combines accurate information with exaggeration, omission, selective framing, or outright falsehood.
Our findings suggest that these gradations matter for belief change: subjective truthfulness differentially predicts belief changes at different levels of objective truthfulness.
Understanding misinformation therefore requires considering not only whether information is true or false, but how true it is and how true it appears as a matter of degree.
This perspective is consistent with evidence that misleading, partially true content can exert greater influence than outright falsehoods (e.g., Allen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This perspective is consistent with evidence that misleading, partially true content can exert greater influence than outright falsehoods (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Allen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings also highlight that beliefs do not always function as representations of objective reality.

Beliefs can serve social, symbolic, and identity-related functions (Sperber, 1975; Van Leeuwen, 2014), meaning that information may influence people even when its factual correspondence with reality is limited.
text.formatted: Beliefs can serve social, symbolic, and identity-related functions <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Sperber, 1975;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Van Leeuwen, 2014)</ref>, meaning that information may influence people even when its factual correspondence with reality is limited.

text.text: A complete account of misinformation should therefore consider both the objective truthfulness of information and the subjective processes through which recipients evaluate and use it.
Three limitations point to directions for future research.
First, LLM ratings provide a scalable proxy for objective truthfulness, but their accuracy depends on the availability, quality, and interpretation of information retrieved through external search.
Future work should therefore triangulate LLM-derived truthfulness ratings with independent, multi-source expert fact-checking, particularly for contested or ambiguous claims.

Second, we examined immediate belief change, leaving open whether the distinction between perceived and objective message truthfulness extends to downstream outcomes such as attitudes, intentions, and behaviour (Velez et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Second, we examined immediate belief change, leaving open whether the distinction between perceived and objective message truthfulness extends to downstream outcomes such as attitudes, intentions, and behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Velez et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should examine whether these effects persist over time and translate into consequential decisions.
Third, our findings are based on relatively short experimental message corpora (no more than 280 characters).

Testing the same framework in more naturalistic information environmentsincluding long-form narratives, social media feeds, and high-identity political debates-would provide a stronger test of generalisability and allow researchers to examine how factors such as source credibility and identity shape the relative contributions of perceived and objective message truthfulness.
Belief change reflects an interplay between subjective perceptions of message truthfulness and objective correspondence with reality.

Here we show that although perceived truthfulness was the stronger predictor of belief change, objective truthfulness made a robust independent contribution and moderated the association between perceived truthfulness and belief change.

People are therefore neither fully divorced from empirical reality nor governed by it alone: belief change depends on both how true a message appears and how closely it corresponds to objective reality.
Considering these two dimensions together provides a more complete account of how socially transmitted information shapes human beliefs.
